mainTopic: Clean versus concise language in the תורה, and stories showing the value of careful, respectful speech.
overview: The גמרא is in the middle of a discussion about how the תורה chooses clean, respectful wording. It finishes explaining why משה's wife is described as 'riding,' then asks the same about אביגיל and gives three answers: fear of the night, fear of דוד, or fear of the steep mountain. Next it asks why the תורה ever writes the blunt word טמא, and sets a rule: clean wording is used only when it is no longer than the blunt wording; otherwise shortness wins, as רב הונא taught, 'always teach your student in a short way.' It tests the rule on אביגיל's verse and answers that רכבת is spelled without a ו, so it is shorter. The גמרא then brings stories about speech: רב refuses to speak with a student who used a crude image, and a student who asked his question cleanly is promised he will become a halachic authority. A כהן who compared his portion to a lizard's tail is found to be flawed, and the גמרא explains how this fits the rule that a serving כהן is not investigated. A story follows of רבי יהודה בן בתירא exposing a gentile who ate the קרבן פסח. The amud ends with two stories about delivering bad news gently: the death of רב כהנא, and יוחנן חקוקאה's poorly chosen hint about the wheat crop.

steps.title: משה's wife rode because of the children
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes answering why משה's wife is described as riding: with small children on board, riding is the normal way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of his children, that is the normal way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to the question about משה's wife. She is described as 'riding' on the donkey, which seems less modest than 'sitting.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier rule was that the תורה uses 'sitting' for women to keep its language modest. משה put his children on the donkey along with his wife. When children are riding along, riding properly is the normal and practical way, so the word 'riding' is not immodest here.

keyTerms.meaning: It is the normal way / standard practice

steps.confusionAlert: This amud begins in the middle of an answer. The question it answers (about משה's wife riding on the donkey) appeared on the previous amud.

phrases.english: Because of his children —
phrases.notes: The children were riding too (שמות ד:כ).

phrases.english: it is the normal way.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם בָּנָיו — אוֹרְחָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to a challenge raised on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Situational exception: the circumstances make riding the normal way.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the Torah broke its own modest-language rule for משה's wife.
steps.terutzMaskana: With children aboard, riding is standard, so the word 'riding' is appropriate.

steps.title: Challenge from אביגיל riding on the donkey
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule from אביגיל, who is described as 'riding' on her donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: 'And she was riding on the donkey'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a verse about אביגיל that says she was 'riding.' She had no children with her, so the previous answer does not help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule says the תורה uses 'sitting' for a woman on an animal. Here a woman is described as 'riding,' with no children involved. So the verse seems to contradict the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? (opens a challenge from a verse)

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
phrases.notes: Here comes a verse that seems to say the opposite.

phrases.english: "And she was riding on the donkey"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָכְתִיב: ״וְהִיא רֹכֶבֶת עַל הַחֲמוֹר״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the answer about משה's wife, a new verse raises the same problem without the 'children' explanation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that the verse uses 'sitting' rather than 'riding' for women.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אביגיל is a woman with no children aboard, yet the verse says 'riding.'

steps.title: First answer: fear of the night
steps.stepSummary: אביגיל rode properly because she was traveling at night, and at night riding securely is the norm.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, because of the fear of the night, it is the normal way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that אביגיל was traveling at night. In the dark it is normal to ride properly for safety.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the children in step 1, this is a special situation. Fear of the dark makes a firm, riding position the normal choice. So the word 'riding' is not immodest here.

phrases.english: There, because of the fear of the night —
phrases.notes: She was traveling in the dark.

phrases.english: it is the normal way.
phrases.notes: Riding securely is standard at night.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, מִשּׁוּם בִּיעֲתוּתָא דְלֵילְיָא — אוֹרְחָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from אביגיל.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביגיל's verse breaks the modest-language rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: Night travel makes riding the normal way, so 'riding' is fitting.

steps.title: Second answer: fear of David
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: night alone would not explain it, but fear of דוד, who was coming to attack, would.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: because of the fear of the night there is no reason, but because of the fear of דוד there is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second possible answer. Night alone may not be enough of a reason. Her fear of דוד was the real reason she rode quickly and securely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד was on his way to destroy נבל's household, and אביגיל rushed out to stop him. Her urgency and fear made fast, proper riding natural. The rule still holds; this is another kind of special circumstance.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces an alternative answer)

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
because of fear of the night — there is no such reason,
because of fear of David — there is.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: מִשּׁוּם בִּיעֲתוּתָא דְלֵילְיָא — לֵיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the 'night' answer with a different reason.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative situational exception (fear of an approaching threat).
steps.terutzMaskana: Fear of דוד explains the riding.

steps.title: Third answer: fear of the mountain slope
steps.stepSummary: A third answer: fear of the steep mountain path made riding properly necessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: fear of דוד also is not a reason, but because of the fear of the mountain there is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third possible answer. She was riding down a mountain, and a steep slope requires a secure riding position.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says she was coming down 'by the covert of the mountain.' Going downhill, sitting sideways is dangerous, so riding astride is the normal way. All three answers share the same idea: special circumstances made riding standard.

keyTerms.meaning: דוד, who was on his way to attack

steps.whatToRemember: All three answers about אביגיל keep the rule intact. Each one points to a special situation (night, דוד, mountain) where riding properly was the normal way.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
fear of David — that too is not a reason,
because of fear of the mountain — there is.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: בִּיעֲתוּתָא דְּדָוִד — נָמֵי לֵיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the 'David' answer with yet another reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fear of דוד explains the riding.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fear of the mountain slope explains the riding.

steps.title: Challenge: the Torah writes the word 'impure'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the תורה uses the blunt word טמא if it always prefers clean language.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't the word 'impure' written in the Torah?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the whole idea that the תורה always uses לשון נקיה. The word טמא appears in the תורה many times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the סוגיא, the גמרא showed that the תורה went out of its way to say 'not pure' instead of טמא. But the תורה also writes טמא directly in many places. So the תורה does not seem to always prefer clean language.

phrases.english: But in the Torah, isn't "impure" written?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְאוֹרָיְיתָא מִי לָא כְּתִיב ״טָמֵא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the riding/sitting examples back to the general principle of clean language.
steps.kashyaTarget: The general claim that the תורה uses לשון נקיה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The תורה frequently writes the blunt word טמא, so it does not always avoid it.

steps.title: The rule: clean language only when it is equally short
steps.stepSummary: The תורה uses clean language when it is the same length; when clean language would be longer, it uses the short wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: wherever they are equal, it speaks in clean language; wherever the words are more numerous, it speaks in short language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens the rule. Clean language is used only when it costs no extra words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two values: לשון נקיה (clean wording) and לשון קצרה (short wording). When the two options are equal in length, the clean one wins. When the clean option is longer (like 'not pure' every time instead of טמא), the תורה chooses the shorter word.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the key principle of the סוגיא: shortness takes priority over clean wording. It explains when the תורה chooses which kind of language.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא: כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּכִי הֲדָדֵי נִינְהוּ —
phrases.english: Rather: anywhere that they are equal (in length) —
it speaks in clean language;
anywhere that the words are more numerous —
it speaks in short language.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּכִי הֲדָדֵי נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about טמא by narrowing the rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תורה always uses clean language.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תורה uses clean language only when it is not longer; otherwise shortness wins.

steps.title: Support: teach your student in a short way
steps.stepSummary: The rule that shortness wins is supported by רב הונא in the name of רב (some say in the name of רבי מאיר): always teach a student concisely.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא said in the name of רב, and some say רב הונא said in the name of רב in the name of רבי מאיר: A person should always teach his student in a short way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its rule with a teaching about how to teach. Short teaching is a recognized value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a teacher should always teach in a short way, it makes sense that the תורה, the ultimate teaching, prefers short wording. That is why shortness can override clean wording. The two versions differ only in who first said it (רב, or רבי מאיר).

phrases.english: As Rav Huna said in the name of Rav,
and some say it as follows,
phrases.notes: A different version of who said it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי מֵאִיר:
phrases.english: Rav Huna said Rav said in the name of Rabbi Meir:

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם יִשְׁנֶה אָדָם לְתַלְמִידוֹ דֶּרֶךְ קְצָרָה.
phrases.english: A person should always teach his student in a short way.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְאָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rule in step 7 that shortness takes priority.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that short wording beats clean wording when they conflict.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב הונא in the name of רב (or רבי מאיר): always teach a student in a short way.

steps.title: Challenge: 'riding' and 'sitting' are the same length
steps.stepSummary: If clean language wins when lengths are equal, why does אביגיל's verse say 'riding' when רוכבת and יושבת are both five letters?
steps.simpleTranslation: And anywhere that they are equal, does it speak in respectful language? But 'riding' and 'sitting' are equal, and yet it says 'riding'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the new rule against אביגיל's verse. The two words have the same length, so the rule says the verse should have used the respectful one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רוכבת (ר-ו-כ-ב-ת) and יושבת (י-ו-ש-ב-ת) each have five letters. By the rule, the תורה should have chosen the respectful 'sitting.' Yet it chose 'riding.'

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that (opens a challenge)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'equal' means equal in number of letters, not in number of words.

phrases.english: And anywhere that they are equal,
does it speak in respectful language?
But "riding" and "sitting"
are equal,
and yet it says "riding"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכׇל הֵיכָא דְּכִי הֲדָדֵי נִינְהוּ מִשְׁתַּעֵי בִּלְשׁוֹן כָּבוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the length rule from step 7 against the אביגיל verse from step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that equal-length options default to respectful language.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רוכבת and יושבת are equal in length, yet the verse picked the less respectful word.

steps.title: Answer: 'riding' is spelled short
steps.stepSummary: In the verse, רכבת is written without a ו, so it has four letters and is shorter than יושבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רכבת is written (without a ו).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word in the verse is spelled without a ו. That makes 'riding' shorter, so the shortness rule chose it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Written as רכבת, the word has four letters while יושבת has five. Since short language wins over respectful language, the verse used רכבת. This confirms the rule from step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written (refers to the spelling in the text)
Written in short spelling, without a ו

steps.whatToRemember: Rule of the סוגיא: when clean or respectful wording costs no extra letters or words, the תורה uses it. When it would be longer, shortness wins. That is why אביגיל's verse uses the short spelling רכבת.

phrases.english: "Riding" is written (without a vav).

steps.triggerLanguage: ״רֹכֶבֶת״ כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge from step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual spelling: the defective spelling makes the word shorter.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רוכבת and יושבת are the same length.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse spells רכבת without a ו, so it is shorter, and shortness takes priority.

steps.title: רב refuses to speak with the student who used a crude comparison
steps.stepSummary: Two students of רב were worn out by a hard topic. One compared their tiredness to a tired 'other thing,' meaning a pig, and the other compared it to a tired young goat. רב would not speak with the first one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two students were sitting before רב. One said: 'This teaching has made us as tired as a tired "other thing" (a pig).' The other said: 'This teaching has made us as tired as a tired young goat.' רב would not speak with the first student.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story to show how much clean speech matters. It is backing up the idea that a person should choose refined words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both students said the same thing: we are exhausted. The only difference was the image each one chose. One picked a pig, an animal Jews avoid even naming, and the other picked a goat. רב's reaction shows that a crude choice of words reveals something about a person, even when the meaning is identical.

keyTerms.meaning: It has made us, it has rendered us
'Something else,' the polite way of saying 'pig'

steps.confusionAlert: Even the crude student never said the word 'pig.' He said דבר אחר, which was already the polite substitute. The problem was not the word. The problem was that he chose a pig as his image at all, when the other student easily picked a clean animal.

phrases.english: There were these two students
who were sitting before Rav.
One said: This teaching has made us
phrases.notes: He means it made them tired.

phrases.english: like a tired 'other thing'
phrases.notes: 'Other thing' is a polite way of saying 'pig.'

phrases.english: And one said: This teaching has made us
like a tired young goat.
And Rav did not speak with that one.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the student who used the pig image.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ תְּרֵי תַלְמִידֵי דַּהֲווֹ יָתְבִי קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the technical discussion of clean language in the תורה, this is a real-life story showing that clean speech matters for people too.
steps.raayaObject: The value of clean, refined speech
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story about רב and two of his students

steps.title: The student who asked his question cleanly is promised he will become a halachic authority
steps.stepSummary: Two students sitting before הלל (one was רבן יוחנן בן זכאי), or according to another version before רבי (one was רבי יוחנן), asked the same question about harvesting grapes and olives. One worded it cleanly and the other bluntly. The teacher predicted that the clean speaker would become a halachic authority, and soon he did.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two students were sitting before הלל, and one of them was רבן יוחנן בן זכאי. Some say they were sitting before רבי, and one of them was רבי יוחנן. One asked: 'Why do we harvest grapes in purity, but we do not harvest olives in purity?' The other asked: 'Why do we harvest grapes in purity, but harvest olives in impurity?' The teacher said: 'I am sure that this one will issue rulings in ישראל.' Only a few days passed before he was issuing rulings in ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story with the same message. This time clean wording earns high praise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both students asked exactly the same halachic question. The first said 'not in purity' and the second said 'in impurity.' Because the first student avoided the word טומאה, the teacher saw that he was fit to be a teacher of the nation, and this was quickly proven true.

keyTerms.meaning: In purity, with pure vessels and hands
I am certain, I am confident
Issues halachic rulings, serves as a halachic authority

steps.confusionAlert: The two students do not disagree about the הלכה. They ask the identical question. The story is only about how each one worded it.

phrases.english: There were these two students
who were sitting before Hillel,

phrases.aramaic: וְחַד מִינַּיְיהוּ רַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי.
phrases.english: and one of them was Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.
And some say: before Rebbi,
and one of them was Rabbi Yochanan.

phrases.aramaic: חַד אָמַר: מִפְּנֵי מָה בּוֹצְרִין בְּטָהֳרָה
phrases.english: One said: Why do we harvest grapes in purity
but we do not harvest olives in purity?

phrases.aramaic: וְחַד אָמַר: מִפְּנֵי מָה בּוֹצְרִין בְּטָהֳרָה
phrases.english: And one said: Why do we harvest grapes in purity
but harvest olives in impurity?
He (the teacher) said: I am certain about this one
that he will issue rulings in Israel.
And not even a few days passed
before he was issuing rulings in Israel.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ תְּרֵי תַלְמִידֵי דַּהֲווֹ יָתְבִי קַמֵּיהּ דְּהִלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story with the same theme. The first story showed a penalty for crude speech, and this one shows a reward for clean speech.
steps.raayaObject: Clean speech marks a person fit for leadership in Torah
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story about the students of הלל, or of רבי

steps.title: The priest who compared his portion to a lizard's tail is found to have a flawed lineage
steps.stepSummary: Three כהנים each described the small share of bread they received. One said a bean, one said an olive, and one said a lizard's tail. They investigated the third כהן's family and found a disqualifying flaw.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were three כהנים. One told the others: 'I received a portion the size of a bean.' Another said: 'I received the size of an olive.' Another said: 'I received the size of a lizard's tail.' They investigated his background and found a trace of disqualification in him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a third story, this time about כהנים. A crude choice of image leads to the discovery of a hidden problem in a כהן's family line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A לטאה is a שרץ, an impure creeping creature. A כהן who reached for an impure image to describe holy bread raised suspicion, and when they checked his lineage they found a פסול. The point is that crude speech can reveal a deeper flaw.

keyTerms.meaning: The tail of a lizard, which is an impure שרץ
A trace of disqualification in his lineage

phrases.english: There were these three priests.
phrases.notes: They were dividing small portions of the showbread.

phrases.english: One said to them: I received a bean-sized portion,
and one said: I received an olive-sized portion,
and one said: I received a portion the size of a lizard's tail.
They investigated his background,
and found in him a trace of disqualification.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ תְּלָתָא כָהֲנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third story on the same theme. Here crude speech leads to the discovery of a real halachic flaw.
steps.raayaObject: Crude speech can reveal a hidden flaw in a person
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story about three כהנים dividing bread

steps.title: Challenge: a priest who served at the altar should not be investigated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the third story using a ברייתא: we do not investigate a כהן's lineage beyond one who served at the מזבח. So how could they investigate a כהן who was already serving?
steps.simpleTranslation: But was it not taught that we do not investigate beyond the מזבח?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem with the story of the three כהנים. It quotes a ברייתא that seems to say this investigation should never have happened. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When checking a family line, once you reach an ancestor who served at the מזבח, you stop, because such a כהן is presumed to be valid. The כהן in the story was himself eating holy bread as a serving כהן, so his lineage should have been beyond question. The challenge is: how could they check him at all?

keyTerms.meaning: But was it not taught (introduces a challenge from a ברייתא)
Beyond the altar, meaning past an ancestor who served at the מזבח

steps.confusionAlert: 'וּלְמַעְלָה' here does not mean physically above the altar. It means going further back in the family line once you have reached a כהן who served at the מזבח.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא sets the rule that service at the מזבח creates a strong presumption that a כהן's lineage is valid. The גמרא now has to explain how the story fits with that rule.

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught:
one does not investigate beyond the altar!
phrases.notes: Once a כהן has served at the altar, his lineage is presumed valid and is not checked further.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא תַּנְיָא אֵין בּוֹדְקִין מִן הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וּלְמַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the investigation in the three-כהנים story could have been allowed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The story that they investigated the lineage of a serving כהן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules that lineage is not checked past a כהן who served at the מזבח. A כהן receiving holy bread was already serving, so investigating him seems to contradict the ברייתא.

steps.title: The flaw found was arrogance, not bad lineage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording of the story. They did not find a שמץ פסול, a flaw in his lineage. They found a שחץ פסול, a flaw of arrogance.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do not read it as 'a trace of disqualification.' Read it instead as 'arrogance of disqualification.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 14. It says the story never claimed they investigated the כהן's family. What they discovered was his arrogant character.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says we do not check the lineage of a כהן who has already served at the מזבח. This answer avoids any conflict, because no lineage check took place. The problem they found was a bad trait (arrogance) shown by his crude, boastful way of speaking, not a family flaw.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Do not say ... rather say': a formula that changes how a word is read
A trace of disqualification, meaning a flaw in lineage
Arrogance that disqualifies, meaning a flaw in character

steps.confusionAlert: שמץ and שחץ sound almost the same. The whole answer depends on switching one word for the other. It is not a new story.

phrases.english: Do not say "a trace of disqualification,"
rather say "arrogance of disqualification."
phrases.notes: The flaw was his haughty character, not his family.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא תֵּימָא ״שֶׁמֶץ פְּסוּל״, אֶלָּא אֵימָא ״שַׁחַץ פְּסוּל״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 14 by rereading one word in the story.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual emendation (changing how a word is read)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: They investigated the lineage of a כהן who was already serving, which goes against the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: They found arrogance in him, not a flaw in his lineage, so the ברייתא is not contradicted.

steps.title: A כהן who insults himself is different
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: even if they did check his lineage, this case is different. The כהן lowered himself with his own words, and that gave them a reason to investigate.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: it is different there, because he cast suspicion on himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, separate answer to the challenge. It keeps the original reading, that they did check his lineage, and explains why that was allowed here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of the ברייתא rests on a normal assumption: a כהן serving at the מזבח was already checked and is fit. This כהן spoke in a way that cast doubt on himself, which weakens that assumption. So this is an exception that comes from his own behavior. The general rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you wish, say': introduces a second, alternative answer
'It is different there': this case is an exception
He lowered or damaged his own standing

steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers to the challenge about the third כהן. (1) What they found was arrogance, not a lineage flaw. (2) He cast doubt on himself, so investigating him was allowed as an exception.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
it is different there,
because he himself cast suspicion on himself.
phrases.notes: His crude comparison to a lizard (a שרץ, which is impure) made people suspicious of him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: שָׁאנֵי הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the same קשיא, in place of the word change in Step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No כהן who has served at the מזבח may ever have his lineage checked.
steps.terutzMaskana: A כהן who casts doubt on himself loses that protection, so he may be investigated.

steps.title: A gentile boasts that he eats the קרבן פסח
steps.stepSummary: A new story about checking lineage. A gentile kept going up to ירושלים and eating the קרבן פסח. He bragged that he ate the best portions even though the תורה forbids him to eat it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain gentile used to go up and eat קרבנות פסח in ירושלים. He said: It is written, 'No foreigner may eat of it,' and 'No uncircumcised man may eat of it,' and yet here I am eating the very best parts!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about investigating who is fit for something holy. This step sets the scene and introduces the gentile's boast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gentile mocks the two verses that forbid a בן נכר and an ערל from eating the קרבן פסח. He thinks he has fooled everyone and even gets the finest meat. That boast sets up the trap that רבי יהודה בן בתירא will use against him.

keyTerms.meaning: The best of the best (the choicest portions)

phrases.english: There was a certain gentile who would go up
and eat Pesach offerings in Jerusalem.
He said: It is written,
"No foreigner may eat of it,"
"No uncircumcised man may eat of it,"
and yet here I am eating
from the best of the best portions.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא אַרְמָאָה דַּהֲוָה סָלֵיק וְאָכֵיל פְּסָחִים בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story of the כהן whose background was checked, the גמרא brings another story about checking someone's background.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the story: a gentile was illegally eating the קרבן פסח and bragging about it.

steps.title: רבי יהודה בן בתירא sets a trap with the אליה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירא asks the gentile whether he was ever fed the אליה, the fat tail. When he says no, the rabbi tells him to ask for it next time. When he asks, the people tell him the אליה goes on the מזבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירא said to him: Did they ever feed you the fat tail? He said: No. The rabbi said: When you go up there, tell them, 'Feed me the fat tail.' When he went up, he told them: 'Feed me the fat tail!' They said to him: The fat tail goes up to God, on the altar.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה בן בתירא pretends that the אליה is the best part, knowing the gentile does not know the הלכה. The gentile follows the advice and asks for the אליה in ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every Jew knows the אליה of a sheep is burned on the מזבח and is never eaten. By asking for it, the gentile shows that he knows nothing about the קרבן פסח. That raises suspicion about who he really is.

keyTerms.meaning: The fat tail of a sheep, which is burned on the מזבח
It goes up to the One Above, meaning it is offered on the מזבח

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה בן בתירא was not really telling him the אליה is permitted to eat. It was a trick to get the gentile to give himself away.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira said to him:
Did they feed you from the fat tail?
He said to him: No.
When you go up there,
say to them: Feed me from the fat tail.
When he went up, he said to them:
Feed me from the fat tail!
They said to him: The fat tail goes up to the Most High.
phrases.notes: It is burned on the מזבח and no person eats it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא: מִי קָא סָפוּ לָךְ מֵאַלְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: the rabbi responds to the gentile's boast with a trap.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The אליה of the קרבן פסח is burned on the מזבח and is not eaten. Asking to eat it shows ignorance.

steps.title: They investigate and expose the gentile
steps.stepSummary: Surprised by the request, the people ask who told him this. He names רבי יהודה בן בתירא. They realize something is wrong, check his background, find out he is a gentile, and execute him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Who told you this? He said to them: רבי יהודה בן בתירא. They said: What is this thing in front of us? They investigated his background, found that he was a gentile, and killed him.
steps.whatsHappening: The odd request makes people suspicious. They know a great חכם like רבי יהודה בן בתירא would never really tell someone to eat the אליה. So they investigate the man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming the rabbi does not help the man. It makes things worse, because the people understand the rabbi must have been sending them a signal. This links back to the theme of checking lineage: a real investigation uncovered someone who did not belong.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is this before us?': an expression of surprise and suspicion

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: מַאן אֲמַר לָךְ הָכִי?
phrases.english: They said to him: Who told you this?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָא.
phrases.english: He said to them: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
They said: What is this matter before us?
phrases.notes: A great rabbi would never really say this, so something must be wrong.

phrases.english: They investigated his background,
and found that he was a gentile,
and they killed him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: מַאן אֲמַר לָךְ הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The trap from Step 18 leads to the investigation and to the gentile being exposed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The gentile's ignorance led to an investigation that revealed who he really was.

steps.title: ירושלים sends thanks to רבי יהודה בן בתירא
steps.stepSummary: The people of ירושלים send רבי יהודה בן בתירא a greeting of peace and praise him. Although he lives far away in נציבין, his 'net' caught the trickster in ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent a message to רבי יהודה בן בתירא: Peace to you, רבי יהודה בן בתירא! You are in נציבין, and your net is spread out in ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the people of ירושלים thanking רבי יהודה בן בתירא for exposing the gentile from far away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'net' is a picture of his clever trap. He lived far off in נציבין, yet he protected the קרבן פסח in ירושלים. Wise words, carefully chosen, helped the community keep its holy things pure.

keyTerms.meaning: Peace to you (a greeting of honor)
נציבין, a city far from ירושלים where רבי יהודה בן בתירא lived

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה בן בתירא used one clever question about the אליה, which is burned on the מזבח and not eaten, to expose a gentile who was eating the קרבן פסח. That earned him the praise: 'You are in נציבין, and your net is spread in ירושלים.'

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָא:
phrases.english: They sent a message to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלָם לָךְ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָא!
phrases.english: Peace to you, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira!
For you are in Netzivin,
and your net is spread out in Jerusalem.
phrases.notes: From far away, his trap caught the deceiver.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָא: שְׁלָם לָךְ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story with the praise sent to the rabbi whose trap worked.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A wise, carefully planned question from רבי יהודה בן בתירא, far away in נציבין, protected the purity of the קרבן פסח in ירושלים.

steps.title: The חכמים send someone to check on the sick רב כהנא
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא fell ill, and the חכמים sent רבי יהושע בריה דרב אידי to find out how he was.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא became sick. The רבנן sent רבי יהושע the son of רב אידי and told him: Go check how he is doing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new story to show how a careful person delivers bad news. This step only sets the scene.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story continues the earlier theme of avoiding harsh or ugly speech. The setup tells us the messenger was sent to bring back a report, so everyone will be waiting for his answer.

keyTerms.meaning: what is his condition (literally 'what is his status')

phrases.english: Rav Kahana fell ill.

phrases.aramaic: שַׁדְּרוּהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי,
phrases.english: The Rabbis sent Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi, to him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: זִיל בְּדוֹק מַאי דִּינֵיהּ.
phrases.english: They said to him: Go check what his condition is.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא חֲלַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new story in the same series of examples about careful speech.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup only: a messenger is sent to report on רב כהנא's condition.

steps.title: He finds רב כהנא has died and signals it without words
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע finds that רב כהנא has passed away. He tears his garment, turns the tear to the back, and returns crying.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and found that רב כהנא had died. He tore his garment, turned the tear around to his back, and came back crying.
steps.whatsHappening: The messenger discovers the sad news and lets his actions show it instead of saying it out loud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tearing the garment (קריעה) is a sign of mourning. Turning the tear to the back made it less obvious, and the crying hinted at the news. He communicates the truth without saying the harsh words himself.

keyTerms.meaning: his soul rested, a gentle way of saying 'he died'
he tore his garment (קְרִיעָה, the mourner's tear)

steps.confusionAlert: He did not hide the tear to deceive anyone. He made the news less jarring and let people figure it out on their own.

phrases.english: He came and found that he had passed away.
He tore his garment,
and turned the tear around to his back,
and he came back crying.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא, אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ דְּנָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by showing what the messenger found and how he reacted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He shows the bad news through mourning actions instead of speech.

steps.title: The רבנן ask whether רב כהנא died
steps.stepSummary: Seeing the signs, the חכמים ask him directly: Did he die?
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Did he pass away?
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן understood the hints and ask the messenger outright. This sets up his careful answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Notice that the רבנן are the ones who put the news into words. The messenger's hints worked, so now he only has to respond.

phrases.english: They said to him: Did he pass away?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A reaction to the signs of mourning in the previous step.

steps.title: I did not say it: a fool spreads bad news
steps.stepSummary: He answers, 'I am not the one saying it,' and quotes the פסוק 'one who spreads bad reports is a fool.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I am not saying it. As the verse says: 'And one who spreads a bad report is a fool' (משלי י:יח).
steps.whatsHappening: The messenger confirms the news without saying it himself and explains why with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads the word דבה (bad report) broadly, as any bad news, not only slander. A wise person avoids being the one who says the painful words. When others draw the conclusion themselves, the truth still comes out.

keyTerms.meaning: I am not the one saying it
one who spreads a bad report

steps.whatToRemember: When bad news must be shared, a careful person lets it be understood indirectly instead of announcing it bluntly.

phrases.english: He said to them: I am not saying it.
"And one who spreads a bad report is a fool."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אֲנָא לָא קָאָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Rabbis' question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He lets them conclude it themselves and says he will not voice bad news, based on the פסוק in משלי.

steps.title: יוחנן חקוקאה hints the wheat failed by praising the barley
steps.stepSummary: Back from the villages, יוחנן חקוקאה is asked about the wheat. He answers that the barley turned out well.
steps.simpleTranslation: יוחנן from חקוק went out to the villages. When he returned, they asked him: Did the wheat turn out well? He told them: The barley turned out well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second story about hinting at bad news. He avoids saying the wheat failed by praising a different crop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the messenger in the first story, he tries to let people work out the bad news themselves. The next step shows that his choice of words was poor.

phrases.english: Yochanan of Chakuk went out to the villages.
When he came back, they said to him:
Did the wheat turn out well?
He said to them: The barley turned out well.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹחָנָן חָקוֹקָאָה נְפַק לְקִרְיָיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second example of hinting at bad news. This time the wording is imperfect.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He hints that the wheat failed by speaking only about the barley.

steps.title: They mock him: go tell the horses and donkeys
steps.stepSummary: They mock his answer, since barley is animal feed, and cite a פסוק from מלכים to prove it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Go announce it to the horses and the donkeys! As it is written: 'The barley and the straw for the horses and the swift steeds' (מלכים א ה:ח).
steps.whatsHappening: The people criticize his answer. Good news about barley matters to animals, not to people who were asking about their food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His hint was indirect, but it was a poor fit. By praising animal feed he made the news sound worse and insulting. The criticism shows that a gentle hint must also be well chosen.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: צֵא וּבַשֵּׂר לַסּוּסִים וְלַחֲמוֹרִים,
phrases.english: They said to him: Go and announce it to the horses and the donkeys,
as it is written: "The barley and the straw for the horses and the swift steeds."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: צֵא וּבַשֵּׂר לַסּוּסִים וְלַחֲמוֹרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Criticizes the wording of his answer in the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: His choice to hint at the bad news by praising barley.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Barley is animal food according to the פסוק, so the 'good news' is useless and even insulting to people.

steps.title: What should he have said instead?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what a better indirect answer would have been.
steps.simpleTranslation: What should he have said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps outside the story to ask what better wording he could have used. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא accepts that hinting was the right approach. The question is only about which hint would have been proper.

phrases.english: What should he have said?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי הֲוֵי לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the criticism by asking for a better way to phrase the answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A proper indirect way to say that the wheat crop failed.

steps.title: Better options: last year's wheat, or the lentils
steps.stepSummary: He could have said that last year's wheat turned out well, or that the lentils, which people eat, turned out well.
steps.simpleTranslation: He could have said: Last year the wheat turned out well. Or alternatively: The lentils turned out well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two better ways he could have hinted at the bad news.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both answers still hint that this year's wheat failed, but neither one insults the listeners. Last year's wheat is still about the same crop. Lentils are food for people, unlike barley.
steps.whatToRemember: Hinting at bad news is good, but the hint must be dignified and fitting. It should point to something relevant to people, not something that sounds insulting.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two stories together teach that careful speech has two parts: avoid saying painful words directly, and choose a hint that is respectful.

phrases.english: Last year the wheat turned out well.
Alternatively: The lentils turned out well.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶשְׁתָּקַד נַעֲשׂוּ חִיטִּין יָפוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of what he should have said.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He could have praised last year's wheat or this year's lentils.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An indirect way of giving bad news should still be relevant and respectful to the listener.
